newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends lower, techs slammed after 3Com warning.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends lower, techs slammed after 3Com warning.

text.p: Wall Street stocks closed lower on Monday as a sweeping sell-off in the technology sector cast a pall over the rest of the market.

Techs were dealt a sharp blow after computer networking company 3Com Corp warned that its third-quarter results would fall short of analysts' estimates. The news triggered a freefall that spread across the sector.
The Dow industrials fell 49 points to close unofficially at 6807. About one-third of the loss was due to International Business Machines Corp, which fell six to 142-3/4.

The Nasdaq Composite slid 22 points to 1335. 3Com was Nasdaq's most active issue, tumbling 13-1/2 to 37-1/4 on more than 36 million shares in volume. Cisco Systems Inc slid 5-1/8 to 58 on 33 million shares traded.

The decline extended a recent slide for major technology companies. Those shares had led the way as the market marched higher but sharply reversed course in the last weeks as concern about their ever-increasing valuations mounted.
"To see so much movement in the blue chip techs is a sign the market's afraid," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Van Kampen American Capital.
"It's a case of people being afraid of a technology sell-off and deciding to ratchet down positions even if they're in them for the long haul," Froehlich said.
Analysts also noted ownership of tech stocks has become more speculative during the latest rally, a factor they said likely contributed to the severity of the decline.

"Trading patterns have shown this money was moving from strong hands to weak hands for several months now," said Harry Laubscher, a market analyst at Tucker Anthony. "In many cases it was moving out of the hands of people who held it on the way up."

Laubscher said such patterns -- during which see "strong handed" institutional holders edge out of positions to take profits as "weak handed" momentum players pour in -- portend turbulent times because the latecomers are more likely to dump positions on any sign of trouble.
Dump they did, in broad selling that pulled in such names as Microsoft Corp, which slipped 2-5/8 to 97-3/4 and Intel Corp, which fell 4-3/4 to 151-5/8. Compaq Computer Corp shed 5-1/4 to 77-3/8.
Beyond the tech sector, the session was a fairly quiet affair, though some retailers did extend their mini-rally.
"Some money appears to be moving to areas like retailers that have not really participated in the rally," Laubscher said.
Sears, Roebuck and Co rose 1-1/2 to 53, Gap Inc gained 3/4 to 32-3/8 and May Department Stores Inc climbed 1-5/8 to 47-1/8.

Among indiviual issues, Westinghouse Electric Corp edged lower after announcing a $1.55 billion stock acquisition of two Gaylord Entertainment Co cable television networks, The Nashville Network (TNN) and Country Music Television (CMT).
Shares in Westinghouse eased 3/8 to 17-3/8, while Gaylord shares fell 3-1/8 to 22-1/4.

ITT Hartford Group Inc jumped 3-1/8 to 78-3/8 after the company announced it would spin off a 20 percent stake in its life insurance business through an initial public offering. Analysts have said such an offering could fetch up to $800 million for the company.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 22.37 to 1335.34.
The S&P 500 index fell 4.13 to 785.43.
The Russell 2000 index of small-cap stocks fell 2.60 to 364.15.
